full_judgment:
This Rule calls in question the legality and propriety of the Order No. 33 dated 20.4.89 passed by learned District Judge, Jhenaidah in Misc. Case No, 26 of 1988 arising out of Title Appeal No. 84 of 1988 rejecting the prayer for restoration of the said title appeal to its file and number. 

 4. An application for restoration of the appeal to its file and number was made under Order 41 rule 19 CPC read with section 151 CPC wherein cause for delay for not taking steps on the date fixed had been stated. That application was registered as Misc. Case No. 86 of 1988. On 29.4.89 Misc Case No. 26 of 1988 was taken up for hearing by the learned District Judge who dismissed the aforesaid Misc. Case ex parte on the ground that the petition for restoration was barred by time. 

 6. This learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff petitioner submits that the order of dismissal of title appeal was illegal and without jurisdiction inasmuch as 17.8.88 was fixed for taking steps by the appellant and it was not fixed for hearing but the learned District Judge without applying his judicial mind dismissed the Misc. Case No. 26 of 1988 on account of not taking steps and as such the order does not come within the purview of rule 17 or 18 of the Order 41 CPC. It is further submitted that as the order of the learned lower appellate Court does not come within the scope of rule 18 of the Order 41, the petition for restoration is liable to be treated as one under section 151 of the CPC. The order of dismissal of Misc. Case No. 26 of 1988 has occasioned failure of justice. 

 7. In reply to this contention the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party submits that the order passed by the learned District Judge refusing to restore the appeal to its file and number on the ground of limitation is perfectly justified inasmuch as order of dismissal was passed on 17.8.88 and the application for readmission of appeal was filed on 22.9.88 and thereby the application filed for readmission of the appeal was out of time by 6 (six) days. It is further submitted that no application under section 5 of Limitation Act seeking condonation of delay was filed with the application and as such the delay was not condoned and the impugned order passed by the learned District Judge rejecting the supplication for readmission of appeal on the ground of limitation does not suffer from any illegality and that the impugned order being in consonance with the provision laid down in Article 168 of the Limitation Act and as such impugned order cannot be held to be contrary to law. The learned Advocate continued to urge that application for readmission of the Title Appeal No. 84 of 1988 was made under Order 41 rule 19 and in support of this contention Annexure 'A' has been put in. The fact that readmission of the aforesaid appeal was sought by filing an application under Order 41 rule 19 CPC is not denied by the learned Advocate for petitioner. The learned Advocate for opposite party urged that there is no general discretion given to the Court to waive the period of limitation or to extend it in hard cases relating to application of section 151 CPC. It is submitted that Order 41 rule 19 CPC read with Article 168 Limitation Act are exhaustive and therefore no inherent power remaining with the High Court to allow the appeals which are time barred and to set aside on order dismissing an appeal under Order 41 rule 19. In support of this contention the decision in the case of Syed Md. Shah Vs. Abdul Jabbar Md. Yakub and others reported in 1943 AIR (Sind) page 132 has been relied upon. The learned Advocate further urged that section 151 CPC cannot enable the Court to break through the provision of Article 168 of the Limitation Act. The object of referring the decision is to show that inherent power cannot be invoked to break through provision of Limitation Act. In the instant case application for restoration of the appeal dismissed for default was made under Order 41 rule 19 CPC and that the Article 168 will govern the application and that the limitation will run from the date of the impugned order. Another decision on which reliance has been placed is reported in SCMR 1975 in the case of Haji Golam Sarwar Vs. Dayaram reported at page 179. In that case his Lordship Hamoodur Rahman the then Chief Justice of Pakistan observed that time for readmission of appeal dismissed for want of prosecution runs from date of dismissal and not from the date of knowledge of dismissal. His Lordship further observed that Article 168 of the Limitation Act begins to run from the date of the dismissal. So it is urged that since the application for readmission of the appeal was made beyond 30 days the learned District Judge was justified in rejecting that prayer for readmission on the ground of limitation. 

 8. In this connection my attention was drawn by the learned Advocate for the appellant petitioner to the decision in the case of Sabitri Bala Vs. Rohini Kanta Mondal reported in 1963 PLD page 25 (Dhaka) but the principle laid down in that decision has no manner of application inasmuch as appeal was dismissed under rules of the Court and not under rules, 11, 17 or 18 of Order 41 CPC. 

 The application filed under Order 41 rule 19 CPC vide Annexure 'A' shows that application was made under the aforesaid rule for readmission of the appeal. Now the only question that calls for determination in this case is whether inherent power can be invoked to have the impugned order set aside. 

 In this connection it may be referred that readmission of the appeal has been sought under provision of Order 41 rule 19. Admittedly no application under section 5 of Limitation Act seeking condonation of delay was filed along with an application for readmission. Even if such application would have been filed no relief could be granted inasmuch as no general discretion has been given to the Court to waive the period of limitation or to extend it in hard cases. Section 5 of Limitation Act does provide for extension of time in certain cases, but this section only applied to appeals or applications to which this section has been made specifically applicable but it does not apply to applications under Order 41 rule 19 CPC. Admittedly no application under section 5 of Limitation Act was filed seeking condonation of delay; even if would have been filed, court did not have the discretion to extend the time. Section 5 of Limitation Act and Article 168 do not apply to application under Order 41 rule 19 CPC inasmuch as Order 41 rule 19 and Article 168 are exhaustive. It has been referred above that in the case of Syed Md. Shah Vs. Abdul Jabar Md. Yeakub and others reported in 1943 AIR (Sind) page 132, it has been held by their Lordships that no inherent power under section 151 CPC can be invoked to have the impugned order set aside and thereby to restore the appeal to its file and number. Thus I am bound to say that provisions of Or. 41 rule 19 are exhaustive and that Order 41 rule 19 read with Article 186 of the Limitation Act will have no application. To hold otherwise would be really an evasion of the definite words of Article 160, Limitation Act. What the learned Advocates for the appellant petitioner asks me to do is to give him a remedy what the Code does not afford and in fact implicitly withholds. If we were to accept the contention that section 151 CPC could be invoked to set at naught any of the provisions of the CPC and that of the Limitation Act, we should give a right of appeal where no such right exists. 

 10. It has already been referred above that in the case of Syed Md. Shah Vs. Abdul Jabar and Ors. reported in 1943 AIR Vol. 30 page 132 their Lordships have held that no inherent power can be invoked under section 151 CPC to have the order for dismissal for default set aside. 

 11. In the case of Bissamal Vs. Kesar Singh and on reported in AIR 1920 (Lahore) page 308 their Lordships held that section 151 cannot enable the court to break through provisions of Limitation Act What happened in that case was that appeal was dismissed for default on 27.1.1919. The application for restoration was put in on 17th November, 1919 and was granted subject to any objection that respondent may have to urge on behalf of the respondent and on behalf of respondent it was urged that application for restoration is time barred under Article 168 of the Limitation Act and that time cannot be extended as section 5 of the Limitation Act is not applicable. On comparing the language employed in Articles 163 and 168 with that of Articles 164 and 169 their Lordships held that the appellant in this case is striving to get benefit which law allows only to defendant or respondent and their lordships further held that inherent power of court cannot be invoked to enable the court to break through clear provision of Limitation Act. So, in the instant case inherent power cannot be invoked to break through Article 168 of Limitation Act and their Lordships was pleased to dismiss the application for readmission of the appeal on the ground of limitation.
